propositions.text: Applicant is a Philippine citizen seeking judicial review of Officer's April 19, 2022 decision denying permanent residence under HCCPC.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, a citizen of the Philippines, seeks judicial review of the decision of an officer with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada [Officer] dated April 19, 2022, in which the Officer denied her application for permanent residence made under the Home Child Care Provider Class [HCCPC].

propositions.text: Officer denied application because Applicant did not meet HCCPC educational requirements.
propositions.quote: The application was denied on the basis that the Applicant did not meet the educational requirements of the HCCPC program.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant, a Philippine citizen, seeks judicial review of the Officer's denial of her HCCPC permanent residence application for lacking educational requirements.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to show Officer's decision was unreasonable or that procedural fairness was denied; judicial review dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I find that the Applicant has not established that the Officer’s decision was unreasonable nor has she established any denial of procedural fairness. Accordingly, the application for judicial review shall be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's decision reasonable and no procedural fairness breach; dismisses judicial review application.

propositions.text: On June 18, 2019, IRCC created HCCP and Home Support Worker classes under IRPA section 14.1.
propositions.quote: On June 18, 2019, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada [IRCC] issued a Ministerial Instruction to create two new classes of permanent residents – the Home Child Care Provider [HCCP] and Home Support Worker classes – pursuant to section 14.1 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act [IRPA].

propositions.text: Section 14.1 allows Minister to establish economic class permanent residents based on economic establishment ability.
propositions.quote: Section 14.1 allows the Minister to establish a class of permanent residents as part of the economic class based on their ability to become economically established in Canada.

propositions.text: HCCPC is part of economic class under IRPR paragraph 70(2)(b).
propositions.quote: The HCCPC is considered to be part of the economic class referred to in paragraph 70(2)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations [IRPR].

propositions.text: Programs provide pathway from temporary to permanent residence for eligible in-home caregiving foreign nationals.
propositions.quote: These two programs were designed to provide a pathway from temporary to permanent residence for foreign nationals in eligible in-home care giving occupations.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains IRCC created HCCP and Home Support Worker classes under IRPA section 14.1 as economic class pathways for eligible in-home caregivers.

propositions.text: HCCPC applicants must have either a Canadian 1-year post-secondary credential or a foreign credential with equivalency assessment within 5 years.
propositions.quote: Among other requirements, applicants to the HCCPC must satisfy the education requirement that they either hold: A Canadian 1-year post-secondary (or higher) educational credential; or A foreign diploma, certificate or credential and an equivalency assessment – issued within five years before the date on which the application is made - that indicates that the foreign diploma, certificate or credential is equivalent to a Canadian educational credential of at least one-year of post-secondary studies.

paragraphs.summary: The court states HCCPC applicants must have a Canadian 1-year post-secondary credential or a foreign credential with a recent equivalency assessment.

propositions.text: Government document sets policy for assessing educational requirements for HCCPC applications.
propositions.quote: The “Home Child Care Provider Pilot and Home Support Worker Pilot: Assessing the application against selection criteria” document published by the Government of Canada sets out the policy, procedures and guidance used by officers to assess applications.

propositions.text: Canadian credential means post-secondary diploma from provincially recognized institution; partial completion insufficient.
propositions.quote: Canadian credentials A post-secondary Canadian educational credential is any post-secondary diploma, certificate or credential that is issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions. As such, an applicant who has started a college or university program and has successfully completed the credits for 1 year of that program, but who has not yet completed the program of study, would not meet this requirement.

propositions.text: Foreign credentials require ECA report showing equivalency to completed Canadian 1-year post-secondary credential, less than 5 years old, from designated organization.
propositions.quote: Foreign credentials For applicants with a foreign educational credential, the ECA report must indicate that the credential is equivalent to a completed Canadian 1-year post-secondary (or higher) educational credential be less than 5 years old on the date of application receipt have been issued on or after the date the ECA organization was designated by IRCC Equivalency assessments will include an assessment by the designated organization of the authenticity of the applicant’s completed foreign educational credentials.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes government policy defining Canadian and foreign credential requirements for HCCPC educational eligibility.

propositions.text: Subsection 73(1) IRPR defines Canadian educational credential and equivalency assessment consistent with policy.
propositions.quote: This is consistent with subsection 73(1) of the IRPR, which defines “Canadian educational credential” and “equivalency assessment” as follows: Canadian educational credential means any secondary school diploma or any post-secondary diploma, certificate or credential that is issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions. equivalency assessment means a determination, issued by an organization or institution designated under subsection 75(4), that a foreign diploma, certificate or credential is equivalent to a Canadian educational credential and an assessment, by the organization or institution, of the authenticity of the foreign diploma, certificate or credential.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes subsection 73(1) IRPR defines Canadian educational credential and equivalency assessment consistent with policy.

propositions.text: ECA reports are issued by IRCC-designated organizations to assess foreign credential equivalency for immigration.
propositions.quote: In order to facilitate this equivalency assessment process for applicants with foreign credentials, an Educational Credential Assessment report [ECA Report] is issued for immigration purposes by an organization designated by IRCC.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains ECA reports are issued by IRCC-designated organizations to assess foreign credential equivalency.

propositions.text: Applicant has no Canadian credentials; obtained WES ECA report evaluating Philippine credentials.
propositions.quote: In this case, as the Applicant does not have any Canadian educational credentials, the Applicant obtained an ECA Report from World Education Services [WES], which is a designated institution.

propositions.text: Applicant's Philippine high school diploma equivalent to Canadian grade 10; university transcript equivalent to secondary diploma plus two years post-secondary study.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s ECA Report indicates two credentials were evaluated. First, her high school or secondary school diploma was evaluated and determined to be the Canadian equivalent of completion of grade 10. Second, the Applicant’s academic transcript from her studies at the University of the East, Caloocan was evaluated and the Canadian equivalency is listed as “secondary school diploma and two years of post-secondary study”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicant's WES ECA report shows Philippine high school diploma equals Canadian grade 10 and university studies equal secondary diploma plus two years post-secondary.

propositions.text: Officer's April 19, 2022 letter rejected Applicant's application for not meeting educational criteria per ECA report.
propositions.quote: On April 19, 2022, the Applicant received a letter advising that her application was rejected as the Officer was not satisfied that the Applicant met the educational criteria.

propositions.text: GCMS notes state ECA report must show equivalency to completed Canadian 1-year post-secondary credential, be less than 5 years old, and from designated organization.
propositions.quote: One of the eligibility requirement for applicants with a foreign educational credentials is that the ECA report must indicate that the credential is equivalent to a completed Canadian 1-year post-secondary (or higher) educational credential be less than 5 years old on the date of application receipt have been issued on or after the date the ECA organization was designated by IRCC

propositions.text: ECA report is conclusive evidence of equivalency to Canadian 1-year post-secondary credential.
propositions.quote: The assessment outcome state in the ECA report is conclusive evidence that an applicant’s completed foreign educational credentials are equivalent to at least a completed Canadian 1-year post-secondary educational credential.

propositions.text: Applicant's ECA report states Canadian equivalency as 'Secondary School Diploma'.
propositions.quote: As per ECA report from WES submitted by PA, they have a Canadian equivalency of “Secondary School Diploma”

propositions.text: Applicant does not meet education requirement and eligibility for HCCPC; application refused.
propositions.quote: PA does not meet the requirement for Education. Therefore PA does not meet the eligibility requirements to apply for permanent residence under the Home Child Care Provider Class. Application refused and letter sent to PA.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker rejected Applicant's application because the ECA report showed only secondary school diploma equivalency, not meeting HCCPC education requirements.

propositions.text: Issues: (i) whether Officer's decision was reasonable; (ii) whether Applicant's procedural fairness rights were breached.
propositions.quote: The following issues arise on this application: (i) whether the Officer’s decision was reasonable; and (ii) whether the Applicant’s procedural fairness rights were breached.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies issues: reasonableness of Officer's decision and procedural fairness breach claim.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review requires decision to be transparent, intelligible, justified, and based on coherent analysis constrained by facts and law.
propositions.quote: When reviewing for reasonableness, the Court must determine whether the decision under review, including both its rationale and outcome, is transparent, intelligible and justified. A reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision-maker [see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 15, 85].

propositions.text: Court intervenes only if decision shows serious shortcomings lacking justification, intelligibility, and transparency.
propositions.quote: The Court will intervene only if it is satisfied there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency [see Adenjij-Adele v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 418 at para 11].

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the reasonableness standard requires transparent, justified decisions and intervenes only for serious shortcomings.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness breaches are reviewable on correctness standard or best reflected by correctness standard.
propositions.quote: breaches of procedural fairness in administrative contexts have been considered reviewable on a correctness standard or subject to a "reviewing exercise ... 'best reflected in the correctness standard' even though, strictly speaking, no standard of review is being applied" [see Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54].

propositions.text: Duty of procedural fairness is variable, flexible, context-specific, assessed by all circumstances including Baker factors.
propositions.quote: The duty of procedural fairness is “eminently variable”, inherently flexible and context-specific. It must be determined with reference to all the circumstances, including the Baker factors [see Vavilov, supra at para 77].

propositions.text: Court asks whether procedure was fair considering all circumstances.
propositions.quote: A court assessing a procedural fairness question is required to ask whether the procedure was fair, having regard to all of the circumstances [see Canadian Pacific Railway Company, supra at para 54].

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness breaches are reviewed on correctness standard and fairness depends on context and circumstances.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer erred by finding she did not meet educational requirements; two years post-secondary study sufficient.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the Officer erred in finding that she did not meet the educational requirements for the HCCPC. The Applicant asserts that her studies at the University of the East were assessed by WES as being the Canadian equivalent to a secondary school diploma and two years of post-secondary study, which is sufficient to meet the requirement of “a foreign diploma, certificate or credential and an equivalency assessment … that indicates that the foreign diploma, certificate or credential is equivalent to a Canadian educational credential of at least one-year of post-secondary studies”.

propositions.text: Applicant asserts Officer ignored or misconstrued evidence of her two years post-secondary study.
propositions.quote: As such, the Applicant asserts that the Officer ignored or misconstrued the evidence before them.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer erred by ignoring evidence that her two years post-secondary study meets educational requirements.

propositions.text: Court rejects Applicant's argument; two years study without conferred credential insufficient for HCCPC educational requirement.
propositions.quote: I reject this assertion and agree with the Respondent that the Applicant’s assertion is premised on a misunderstanding of the educational requirements. Though the ECA Report states the Applicant had completed the equivalent of two-years of post-secondary study, it was not evidence that the study resulted in conferment of a credential that would be equivalent to a Canadian credential (specifically a diploma, certificate or credential that is equivalent to a one-year Canadian educational credential with at least one year of post-secondary studies). Completing years of study without the conferment of a credential is not enough to meet the educational requirement of the HCCPC, as is made clear in the “Home Child Care Provider Pilot and Home Support Worker Pilot: Assessing the application against selection criteria” document cited above. An applicant must have received an actual credential, such as a diploma or certificate. As there was no evidence of a conferred credential, the Officer reasonably determined that the Applicant had failed to meet the educational eligibility requirement.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds two years of study without a conferred credential does not meet HCCPC educational requirements; Officer's decision reasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer may not have properly considered ECA Report as GCMS notes omit two years post-secondary study.
propositions.quote: The Applicant further asserts that the Officer may not have properly considered the ECA Report as the GCMS notes make no reference to her two years of post-secondary studies, which calls into question the reasonableness of the decision.

propositions.text: Court rejects this; Officer is presumed to have considered all evidence and referenced credentials relevant to eligibility.
propositions.quote: I also reject this assertion. The Officer is assumed to have considered all of the evidence when making their decision and in this case, the Officer expressly referenced the ECA Report. Moreover, the Officer’s notes made reference to the credentials that the Applicant had (as opposed to all of her education). Given that the educational eligibility requirement is focused on credentials, this reference in the Officer’s GCMS notes was sufficient for the purpose of establishing the reasonableness of their decision.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues Officer ignored part of ECA Report; court rejects, finding Officer considered relevant credentials and decision reasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant asserts Officer breached procedural fairness by not giving opportunity to respond via interview or fairness letter.
propositions.quote: The Applicant further asserts that the Officer breached the Applicant’s procedural fairness rights by not giving her an opportunity to respond to the Officer’s concerns, either by way of an interview or a procedural fairness letter.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant alleges procedural fairness breach by Officer's failure to provide response opportunity.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness in permanent residence applications is low; no obligation to notify deficiencies or provide opportunity to address them unless credibility concerns arise.
propositions.quote: This Court has recently confirmed the requirements of procedural fairness in the context of applications for permanent residence under the Canadian Experience Class [CEC], which I find applies equally to an application for permanent residence under the HCCPC. Specifically: An applicant has the onus of providing sufficient evidence to support a positive decision on the application. The degree of procedural fairness owed to an applicant under the CEC program is at the low end of the spectrum. There is no obligation on a decision maker to notify an applicant of deficiencies in the application or supporting documentation. There is no obligation on a decision maker to provide an applicant with an opportunity to address any concerns that supporting documents are incomplete, unclear or insufficient to satisfy the decision maker that the applicant meets the legal requirements governing the application. If a decision maker has concerns relating to the credibility of information submitted in support of an application or to the accuracy or genuineness of that information, procedural fairness will often require that the applicant be given an opportunity to address those concerns.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains low procedural fairness duty in permanent residence applications unless credibility concerns arise.

propositions.text: Officer had no credibility concerns and found evidence insufficient; no obligation to provide opportunity to address deficiencies; no procedural fairness breach.
propositions.quote: As the Officer expressed no concerns and made no findings regarding the credibility of the information submitted by the Applicant but rather found that the evidence submitted did not satisfy the educational requirements, there was no obligation upon the Officer to provide the Applicant with an opportunity to address the deficiency in her evidence. Accordingly, I find that there was no breach of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no procedural fairness breach as Officer had no credibility concerns and no duty to provide opportunity to address evidence deficiencies.

propositions.text: Officer's decision supported by evidence and not unreasonable; no procedural fairness denial; judicial review dismissed.
propositions.quote: As the Officer’s decision was supported by the evidence before them, I cannot conclude that the Officer’s decision was unreasonable. Moreover, the Applicant has not demonstrated any denial of procedural fairness. Accordingly, the application for judicial review shall be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Officer's decision was reasonable and no procedural fairness breach; dismisses judicial review.

propositions.text: No question for certification arises; judicial review dismissed.
propositions.quote: Neither party proposed a question for certification and I agree that none arises. JUDGMENT in IMM-4140-22 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application for judicial review is dismissed. There is no question for certification.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no question for certification and dismisses the judicial review application.
